title: Persistence
summary: Persistence is the collection of mechanisms an intruder uses to retain access across reboots, password changes, session expiry and partial remediation, so that initial access does not have to be won again. Host-based persistence attaches to legitimate startup behaviour: autostart entries, scheduled tasks, system services, logon scripts, shell profiles, and browser or office extensions. Identity-based persistence is often more valuable and harder to see, because it lives in the directory or cloud tenant rather than on an endpoint; examples include newly created accounts, added credentials or keys, modified federation settings, and application registrations with delegated permissions that outlive any single session. Network-based persistence covers configurations that survive host rebuilds, such as remote access profiles, tunnels and backup channels. Every mechanism trades stealth against resilience, and defenders can exploit that trade-off: the more durable the mechanism, the more likely it is to touch a monitored location, generate an audit record, or require a privileged change. Practical detection therefore starts from an accurate baseline of what is allowed to autostart, which scheduled tasks and services normally exist, and which principals hold privileged roles. Deviations from that baseline, combined with audit events for account creation, permission grants and application registration, give far better coverage than hunting for specific tools. Mitigation combines application control, privileged access management with approval workflows, credential hygiene, and centralised logging that an intruder cannot quietly edit.
objectives: You will be able to categorise persistence mechanisms as host-based, identity-based or network-based.
You will be able to explain the trade-off between resilience and stealth for common autostart mechanisms.
You will be able to build a baseline of legitimate autostart locations, services and scheduled tasks.
You will be able to spot tenant-level persistence through account creation, credential addition and application registration.
You will be able to recommend controls that make durable access expensive for an intruder.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

beginner.definition: Persistence means the methods an intruder uses to keep access after a reboot, a password change, or a partial cleanup. Without it, a single restart could end the intrusion. Persistence can live on a machine, inside an identity system, or in the network itself. It exists so the intruder does not have to break in a second time.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you remove the intruder but leave their persistence behind, they simply come back. This is why cleanups sometimes fail and the same incident reappears weeks later. Persistence often hides in normal startup behaviour, such as scheduled tasks or service accounts, so it looks ordinary. You cannot spot what is unusual unless you first know what is normal. A written baseline of allowed startup items, tasks and admin accounts is your best defence.
howItWorks: After getting in, the intruder looks for places that start programs automatically.
They add their access to an autostart entry, a scheduled task, or a service.
They may also create a new account or add a key in the identity system.
Now the access returns whenever the machine restarts or the user logs in.
Even if you close the first opening, their quiet back door stays open.
beginner.example: Suppose you change the locks on your front door after a break-in. You feel safe again. But the intruder copied a key and hid it under a garden stone. They return a month later without forcing anything. Replacing the lock alone did not help, because the copy was never found. Persistence works exactly like that hidden key. Cleaning up the visible entry point is not enough; you must also find the copies.
takeaways: Removing the intruder is not enough; you must remove their persistence.
Know which programs and tasks are allowed to start automatically.
New accounts and newly added access keys are persistence as well.
